searchText: > Fair. I was looking to be symbolic of a “merge.” Ironically Berlin would have actually worked really well 🤣 Or Istanbul. It sits on two continents. It was the capital of the Byzantine empire, etc 🙂 Just to keep this channel a bit more technical, please use the EthMagicians thread to discuss this further 🙂 https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/ethereum-roadmapping-improvements/6653/20 On discussion regarding block numbering after the merge - my main focus was on how to solve: Alice: "I sent you X ETH on block #10000000" Bob: "There is no such block"/"The block doesn't contain the transaction" So not focusing on power users, as there probably will not be problems getting familiar with two numbers (Execution layer `block_number` and Consensus layer slot number). But for regular users maybe we can try to expose the `block_number` as the main number. This "discounts" the importance of the Consensus layer a bit as slot number would not be seen as *the main number*, but overall it looks like a solution that would not confuse regular users. There still would be some UI/UX challenges, for example, explorers maybe should show only non-empty slots by default (nice sequence of `block_numbers`), however, there should be an option to see empty slots too. Anyway, I think somebody could try to reach regular users and ask which way looks less confusing. Why would you use block numbers rather than transaction hashes for transaction identification? Blocks have many transactions, so a block number by itself isn't a lot of use. Although if you wanted to you could continue to use the execution layer block number. This example was an oral conversation, but my main point is that block numbers are exposed widely. So users will be very confused if after merge they see slot numbers Is there any reason we would call the thing the consensus engine produces anything other than a slot? Or does the consensus engine have blocks and slots as separate things? Would it be accurate to say that the consensus engine produces slots, and some subset of those slots are filled with execution engine blocks? Or is it more correct to say that the consensus engine has slots that are filled with consensus blocks, which include execution blocks within them? A slot is just a 12-second period of time. But from the consensus layer it's all pretty irrelevant, as the format of the chain would be the same. This last statement is correct And that’s where is the confusion. As there will be consensus block #1000 that will contain execution block #500000 Yeah, it may make sense to harmonize the block number post-merge fwiw, beaconchai.in doesn't show "numbers" for blocks right now Consensus block “number” is probably not a right term, it’s actually slot number. beaconcha.in shows slot numbers I really think that the consensus side should be ignored for the execution layer. In future we're going to have shards managed by the execution layer, so attempting to synchronize numbers is not going to work long-term. Yeah, I was convinced on the call that synchronizing numbers probably won't work. I do think we need some solution though, or there will be a lot of confusion for people. And likely some number of bugs introduced as well. I don't see that; the consensus layer is unlikely to show up on users' radar at all. My suggestion would be to mainly expose ‘block_number’ and keep slot number as a technical field, so no need for synchronisation. Hashes will be easier as it’s collision resistant so when users will mix hashes from both chains it will be often possible resolve it via UI. Slot information is never exposed to the execution layer, as far as I am aware. I’m more about regular users checking things on explorer I think it is dangerous to make assumptions about what will ultimately be exposed to users and what users will use. From a UX design standpoint, I would not have expected block numbers, blocks, hashes, etc. To be exposed to users of a database. Yet, that is the world me live in, where for reasons that aren't clear these complexities were never abstracted away from the user. If we end up in that world then it could be called 'consensus block number' to differentiate. I agree with <@144468805697929216> and just wanted to stress that: users and stakers have very different profile. Consensus slot will only be relevant to the latter, just as difficulty is only relevant to miners now and not to the rest of the world. Block number `X` will continue to mean execution block `X` to most, and when it actually is meant to be a consensus block in slot `X` then the interlocutor will be a staker/dev that will know this

excerpts.author: sauliusgrigaitis
excerpts.content:
On discussion regarding block numbering after the merge - my main focus was on how to solve: 

Alice: "I sent you X ETH on block #10000000"
Bob: "There is no such block"/"The block doesn't contain the transaction"

So not focusing on power users, as there probably will not be problems getting familiar with two numbers (Execution layer  `block_number` and Consensus layer slot number). But for regular users maybe we can try to expose the `block_number` as the main number. This "discounts" the importance of the Consensus layer a bit as slot number would not be seen as *the main number*, but overall it looks like a solution that would not confuse regular users. There still would be some UI/UX challenges, for example, explorers maybe should show only non-empty slots by default (nice sequence of `block_numbers`), however, there should be an option to see empty slots too. Anyway, I think somebody could try to reach regular users and ask which way looks less confusing.

Why would you use block numbers rather than transaction hashes for transaction identification?  Blocks have many transactions, so a block number by itself isn't a lot of use.

Although if you wanted to you could continue to use the execution layer block number.
